BOOK ENTRY

SOURCE EXCERPTS FROM THE BOOK EXPLAINING AND DEMONSTRATING ITS METHOD
SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/01-introduction.adoc — opening

Shortly after feeding the five thousand, Jesus gave a hard teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum (John 6:59): “Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you… He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him” (John 6:53, 56).
After He said this, many of His disciples murmured — “This is an hard saying; who can hear it?” — and “from that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him” (John 6:60, 66).
It was so bad that Jesus turned to the twelve and asked whether they would also go away.

It was a hard saying because those who heard it did not know the symbolic language of the scriptures, and took it over-literally, saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John 6:52).
Which prompts the question: why would Jesus speak in a manner that drives people away?
Why not speak plainly?

He did it to fulfill the Scriptures, which prophesied that He would speak in parables.
When he spoke publicly he always used parables — “without a parable spake he not unto them” (Matthew 13:34) — and only with his closest disciples did he explain their meaning.
Even so, when he gave the parables of the kingdom his own disciples did not understand, and Jesus rebuked them for it. The rebuke was fair because the keys were already in the Old Testament: the “dark sayings of old” the psalm said he would utter (Mark 4:13; Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35). That exam waits a chapter ahead: The Parables of the Kingdom. [Footnote: The Parables of the Kingdom chapter derives each parable of Matthew 13 from the Old Testament alone.]

In other words, scripture prophesied that the message would be encrypted in parables and decoded with the Old Testament.
If you think you can read the New Testament without an intimate understanding of the Old, chances are you will walk away like the masses — either by interpreting it in a way you reject, or by misinterpreting it in a way you can accept, and facing the same consequences either way.

The first hearers of the apostles knew better.
When Paul preached in Berea, Luke recorded how the hearers received him — and graded them for it:

These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.

They tested Paul against the Old Testament, and Scripture calls that nobility.
How many today search the Old Testament to see whether their understanding of Paul is true?
The order has quietly reversed: Paul, as we understand him, has become the judge of the very scriptures he was judged by.
And the test is not for Paul only — your understanding of any verse must be tested against every other verse, for “at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15): one verse cannot make a doctrine.

The Bible provides two symbolic words, meat and milk, to describe its teachings, and if you do not do the work to churn the milk into meat, you will remain immature at best — and at worst turn away entirely, like the crowds in Jesus’ day.

The purpose of this book is to teach you how I learned to chew the word of God and test everything.
It is a repeatable, reproducible process that has yielded more pearls of wisdom — and more appreciation for the supernatural structure of the word of God — than I could possibly fit in one book.
We will go through the process systematically and apply it to dozens of symbolic words, starting with meat and milk.
But first we must prepare the ground by explaining the difference between a word and a symbol.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — opening through How the Exam Is Taken

At the end of the seven parables of the kingdom, Jesus gave His hearers an exam of one question, and they passed it: “Yea, Lord.”
It had not started that way.
At the first parable — the key to all of them — His own disciples stumbled, and He rebuked them: “Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables?” (Mark 4:13).

Stop and weigh that rebuke.
A teacher may not be astonished that students fail an exam on material they were never given; His astonishment is only just if the answers were already on the table.
They were, and He said where.

The psalm He fulfills by teaching in parables locates the material in the past, not the future: “I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old: which we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us” (Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35).
And the Scriptures the disciples grew up on do not merely contain parables — they decode them in front of the reader and expect him to grade himself.

Nathan told David a story about a ewe lamb; David judged its villain to death without seeing his own face — “the man that hath done this thing shall surely die” (2 Samuel 12:5) — and Nathan handed him the key in four words: “Thou art the man” (2 Samuel 12:7).
Isaiah sang a parable of a vineyard, then handed over the key: “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7).
Ezekiel told a riddle of two eagles and a vine, and God's next word is the very question Jesus would ask on the boat: “Know ye not what these things mean?” — followed by the answer, “the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem” (Ezekiel 17:2, 12).

The exam is closed-book in one direction only: everything needed sits in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.
Take each parable, then, the way a disciple on the shore had to take it — derive the meaning from the Scriptures he already had, write it down, and only then let the Teacher grade the work.
That is how this chapter will read them, and it will keep score.
More broadly, it will establish the principle of how to decode all of Scripture using the full body of the word.

Before the first parable, fix the procedure, because it is this book's whole method in miniature.
Take the parable's own words — sower, seed, ground, thorns, fowls — and search the Scriptures for the same words and phrases, everywhere they fall.
Where Scripture has already defined a term out loud — Isaiah's own key, above: the vineyard is the house of Israel — that definition is not local color for one passage; it holds, and it holds uniformly, or parables could not be decoded at all.

Next, weigh what you gathered before you lean on it.
One verse makes a candidate, not a key: a symbol is established when the pattern spans Moses and the prophets and the psalms — independent witnesses carrying the same figure, with no counter-text standing against them.
That standard is what makes the rebuke in the boat just, and it measures its weight: Jesus did not upbraid the twelve for missing an obscurity; seed and ground and thorns and fowls were established patterns, laid down across the whole of the Scriptures read to them every sabbath since childhood.
The better attested the pattern, the more accountable the hearer.

The difference between their seat and yours matters.
The disciple on the shore had his memory and the weekly reading; you have the whole text searchable in moments — a concordance, a search bar, and tools that can gather every use of a word while you frame your next question.
Recall was never the point of the exam, and now it is not even the obstacle: the test is not whether you remember the matches, but whether you go look for them.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — The Sower, Derived and Graded

“Behold, a sower went forth to sow” (Matthew 13:3).
Close the Gospels; what could a hearer of Moses and the prophets make of that?
Start with the seed, which Isaiah had defined in one breath with the rain:

For as the rain cometh down… that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: so shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth…

The word is the seed to the sower and the bread to the eater — one verse, both figures.
And Moses had sung the same rain long before: “My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew” (Deuteronomy 32:2) — what falls from heaven to make the ground bear is teaching.

Next the ground.
Jeremiah had already preached this parable as a command: “Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns” — and his very next sentence names the soil: “take away the foreskins of your heart” (Jeremiah 4:3-4) — plowing and circumcising, one operation in two figures: remove the blocking flesh so the seed can enter.
Hosea gives the same order in the same words: “break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD” (Hosea 10:12).
The ground is the heart, and the thorns were choking Judah's heart seven centuries before the sermon by the sea — and the thorns have a pedigree older still, for they are the curse-ground's own crop: “thorns also and thistles shall it (the ground) bring forth to thee” (Genesis 3:18), what the cursed earth grows where food should stand.

Now derive what the thorns mean, for the Old Testament assigns that too.
Read the sentence they grow in: the same curse that gives the ground its thorns sentences the man to anxious toil for his bread — “in sorrow shalt thou eat of it… in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Genesis 3:17, 19) — the thorns spring up in the field of the struggle for a living.
And that pair of weeds — thorn and thistle together — returns exactly once more in the Hebrew Scriptures, and Hosea builds the whole indictment around it:

Israel is an empty vine, he bringeth forth fruit unto himself: according to the multitude of his fruit he hath increased the altars; according to the goodness of his land they have made goodly images.
Their heart is divided; now shall they be found faulty…

The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us.

Increase, a divided heart, and the curse-ground's own crop sprouting on the altars: riches choking the heart is Hosea's picture before it is the parable's.

Isaiah's vineyard tells the same story, and he graded it himself.
The vineyard planted with the choicest vine gave wild grapes instead, and the sentence fell:

And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.

Isaiah then hands over the key:

For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry.

The vineyard is Israel, and its briers and thorns are men — the woes that follow name them, person by person:

Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!

Here is the monopoly-builder — buying house after house and field after field until no one else has a place, alone in the middle of everything he has swallowed.

Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!
And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.

Here is the pleasure-lover — feasting from morning drink to evening music, past all notice of God.
Riches and pleasures came up where fruit should have stood: Isaiah graded the thorns seven centuries before the sermon by the sea.

Even the stony ground was on record, for the heart God promises to replace is “the stony heart” (Ezekiel 36:26).
And why is the exchange a heart of flesh for a heart of stone?
Because flesh is ground: adam was formed “of the dust of the ground,” adamah (Genesis 2:7) — the man is named for the soil he is — and he was sent forth “to till the ground from whence he was taken” (Genesis 3:23), so the Sower's field was staked out in Eden.
No one plows rock — “will one plow there with oxen?” (Amos 6:12) — and the very oracle that promises the heart of flesh promises its plowing: “I am for you… and ye shall be tilled and sown” (Ezekiel 36:9).
The seed that found “no deepness of earth” on stone takes root in flesh: the law once carved on “tables of stone” written now “in fleshy tables of the heart” (2 Corinthians 3:3) — “ye are God's husbandry” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

What does ground bring forth when the seed takes?
Grass — “all flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6) — a symbol with a chapter of its own.

What of the fowls that devour the wayside seed?
The first time birds descend on a covenant in Scripture, they come as devourers: “when the fowls came down upon the carcases, Abram drove them away” (Genesis 15:11) — uninvited, snatching at the covenant sacrifice, driven off by the covenant man.
In Egypt, Joseph heard a dream of birds eating baked bread out of a basket and graded it without hesitation as a sentence of death (Genesis 40:17-19).
Birds that snatch what was given out of its place are the enemy's agents; a boy raised on Genesis could have written that down.

.The Teacher grades the derivation

|===
| Element | Derived from the Law and the Prophets | The Teacher's key

| Seed
| The word — rain-borne seed, rain-borne doctrine (Isa 55:10-11; Deut 32:2)
| “The seed is the word of God” (Luke 8:11)

| Ground
| The heart — plowed, circumcised, tilled and sown (Jer 4:3-4; Hos 10:12; Ezek 36:9, 26; Gen 2:7)
| The word “sown in his heart” (Matt 13:19)

| Fowls
| The devourers on the covenant and on the bread (Gen 15:11; 40:17-19)
| “Then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown” (Matt 13:19)

| Thorns
| The curse-crop; riches dividing the heart (Gen 3:17-19; Hos 10:1-8; Isa 5:6-12)
| “The care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word” (Matt 13:22)
|===

Four for four — Isaiah's answer, Jeremiah's, Abram's, Hosea's — and not one of the four needed a word Jesus had not yet spoken.
His astonishment in Mark 4:13 was just.

Yet let me be fair, for I would have fared no better.
Handed the parable with no Bible in reach, I would have failed it as completely as any man on the shore.
With a Bible and a printed concordance — and the assurance that the answer was in there somewhere — the derivation above might have cost me days, or months.
It is only with modern tools that I can derive the interpretation independently at all, without leaning on any man's commentary.

Daniel was told to seal the words “even to the time of the end,” when “many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased” (Daniel 12:4).
The running to and fro is through the scriptures themselves — and the knowledge increased is this.

SOURCE: books/symbolic-language/43-garments.adoc

A man is bound hand and foot and thrown out of a wedding feast into the dark — and his offense was his clothing.
The feast is no ordinary supper: it is a king’s, made “for his son” (Matthew 22:2) — a parable of the kingdom, and the wedding is the marriage of the Lamb.

The man “had not on a wedding garment” (Matthew 22:11), and when the king asks how he entered so, he has no answer; “he was speechless” (Matthew 22:12) — the Greek is stronger than the English: phimoō, to muzzle, the same word Paul uses of the ox that treads out the grain (1 Corinthians 9:9) and the very word Jesus speaks to the storm and to unclean spirits, “Peace, be still” (Mark 4:39), “Hold thy peace” (Mark 1:25).
He was not merely at a loss for words; he was muzzled — silenced the way a power greater than his own silences what it overrules, with no defense in his mouth because he had none on his back.

He was not stopped at the gate — he was invited, seated, and only then found out, for “many are called” (Matthew 22:14).
What condemns him is what he has on.
At that very marriage Scripture halts to name the garment.

And it was given unto her that she should array herself in fine linen, bright and pure: for the fine linen is the righteous acts of the saints.

The fine linen is the righteous acts of the saints — the things they did.
The Greek is dikaiōmata, righteous deeds, and the ASV, ESV, NASB, and NIV all render it so.
The King James shortens it to “the righteousness of saints,” and on that one narrowed word a long confusion is built: righteousness gets turned from something you do into a state you merely have, sanctification folded into justification until the garment seems to require no weaving at all.
But the word is plural and active — righteous acts.

The garment is righteousness performed; to be clothed is to have done it, to be bare is to stand in your sins.
Nor is the doing self-made: the verse's first clause says the linen “was given unto her” — deeds God “hath before ordained that we should walk in them” (Ephesians 2:10) — granted, then worn.
So the man who came to the wedding with no garment came with no righteous acts on him at all — invited, seated, and naked.

Scripture says plainly what those acts are, for righteousness is itself a word men stumble over — taken for a vague goodness, or a verdict merely received.
The law has already defined it: righteousness is the commandments observed and done (Deuteronomy 6:25; Psalm 119:172).
Lest anyone make it a state without deeds, John says it in one line: “he that doeth righteousness is righteous” (1 John 3:7).
Righteousness is the doing of what God commanded — so the garment of righteous acts is simply the law kept, and worn.

This is why the song over this chapter sings the way it does: “he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness” (Isaiah 61:10) — garments of yeshuah: the covering He gives is salvation-wear, and its fabric is righteousness.
And it is the robe the father calls for when the prodigal comes home: “Bring forth the best robe, and put it on him” (Luke 15:22) — the covenant covering restored on repentance, before the boy can finish his speech.

Behind the garment stands the covenant.
When God first took Israel for His own, He told it as the clothing of a naked foundling:

…I spread my skirt over thee, and covered thy nakedness… and entered into a covenant with thee… and thou becamest mine.

Three phrases for one act: to spread the skirt, to cover the nakedness, to enter the covenant.
That spread skirt is the kanaph, the wing, doing both of its offices: the edge that carries the fringe bound as the reminder to keep the commandments and do them (Numbers 15:39), and the shade a refuge shelters under. [Footnote: The kanaph — wing, skirt, border, corner — and the fringe at its edge are derived in the Wings chapter.]
The covenant contains the commands; faithfulness to them gains the covering — and what it covers is the nakedness, the sin.

What follows is a second gift, given inside the covenant:

Then washed I thee with water; yea, I throughly washed away thy blood from thee, and I anointed thee with oil.
I clothed thee also with broidered work… and I girded thee about with fine linen…

First the covering of the covenant; then the clothing of the covered.
Revelation keeps the same grammar at the wedding — “to her was granted that she should array herself” (Revelation 19:8): given, and put on by her; deeds God “before ordained that we should walk in them” (Ephesians 2:10), worked in her by His word, and washed whiter than snow when she stains them.

The righteous acts that make up the garment, then, are not scattered good turns — they are the covenant lived out, the law kept and worn where every eye can see it.
As the name is the covenant owned, the garment is the covenant worn.

The first garment was cut at the cost of blood.
The man and his wife stood naked by their sin, and God makes them “coats of skins” and “clothed them” (Genesis 3:21) — a covering that cost a life, the first blood shed to clothe the guilty, and the first shadow of the Lamb to come.
So nakedness is a symbol in its own right, the exact opposite of the garment: the clothed are covered by covenant, the naked stand exposed in their breach — and every verse that defines the one defines the other.

The garment is woven of righteous acts, and the acts themselves are clean — but the cloth can be soiled.
One verse is pressed into service to deny this:

But we are all as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags…

It is read as if obedience itself were filth — as if the more law a man keeps, the dirtier he grows.
But read the whole line: “we are all as an unclean thing,” and so even “our righteousnesses” come out stained.
It is not the righteous act that is filthy; it is the sin it is worked in.
The rag is blood-stained — fouled by the very iniquities the verse goes on to name — not because doing right is wrong, but because the doer is unclean.
A clean deed from a stained hand comes away marked.

The answer to a dirty garment is not to take it off; it is to wash it. “Wash you, make you clean,” God says in the same prophet, and then, “though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:16-18).
The saints “washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Revelation 7:14); Joshua the high priest stands “clothed with filthy garments” until the word goes out, “Take away the filthy garments from him… I will clothe thee with change of raiment” (Zechariah 3:4) — the iniquity removed, the robe made clean.
The keeping is itself commanded: the last beatitude in Scripture is for “they that do his commandments, that they may have right to the tree of life” (Revelation 22:14).
Those who take no responsibility for their robe — who neither weave nor wash — are the ones found bare.

The Lord enacted it the night before He died.
He girded a towel and washed the disciples’ feet, and when Peter refused, He warned, “If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me” (John 13:8).
Then the key:

He that is washed needeth not save to wash his feet, but is clean every whit.

The bath is baptism — washed once into the Name, and so into the covenant: “as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27).
A man is not bathed again and again; he is not baptized over and over, and the robe is put on once.

Yet his feet gather the dirt of the road and must be washed — the feet are the walk, the conduct that is a man’s way.
Jesus therefore stooped to wash them: not a second baptism, but the daily cleansing of the walk that keeps the garment clean.
And “ye also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13:14).

There is an opposite error, and it is the older one.
In the garden the man and his wife “sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons” (Genesis 3:7) — a covering of their own cut and their own measure, what was right in their own eyes.
Scripture marks that road: “There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death” (Proverbs 14:12); “Every way of a man is right in his own eyes: but the LORD pondereth the hearts” (Proverbs 21:2).

God strips the fig leaves off and clothes them Himself, at the cost of blood.
The covering must be cut to His pattern, not to ours.

The fig tree itself shows what such a covering is worth.
Jesus came to one “having leaves” and “found nothing thereon, but leaves only”; He cursed it — “Let no fruit grow on thee henceforward for ever” — and it withered away (Matthew 21:19; Mark 11:13-14).
The leaves are the show; the fruit is the substance.
A tree hung with leaves and bearing no fruit is the fig-leaf covering in one picture — the look of righteousness where the works God came seeking are not.
He is not fed by leaves; He looks for fruit.

A garment given can still be defiled, so it must be kept.
The Lord commends the few in Sardis “which have not defiled their garments,” and promises “they shall walk with me in white” (Revelation 3:4); Jude speaks of “hating even the garment spotted by the flesh” (Jude 23); and the watchword for the last hour is just this:

Behold, I come as a thief.
Blessed is he that watcheth, and keepeth his garments, lest he walk naked, and they see his shame.

To keep the garment is to go on doing the righteousness it is made of.
This is why the apostles speak of it as something you put on: “put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 13:14); “put on the new man,” and with him “bowels of mercies, kindness… meekness, longsuffering” (Colossians 3:10-12); as Job said long before, “I put on righteousness, and it clothed me” (Job 29:14).
The clothing is conduct.

The wardrobe is God’s own: Isaiah watched Him dress — “he put on righteousness as a breastplate, and an helmet of salvation upon his head” (Isaiah 59:17) — and Paul issues the same suit to the soldier: the breastplate of righteousness, the helmet of salvation, truth for a belt and the word for a sword (Ephesians 6:14-17).
The armour of God is not a figure borrowed from Rome; it is God’s own clothing from the prophets, lent to the man who will wear it.
A robe is not framed and admired; it is worn, kept clean, and worn again tomorrow.

To be without the garment is to be naked, and nakedness, from the garden onward, is not nudity but exposure — the covenant covering gone, the shame seen.
Laodicea is “wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked” and does not feel it (Revelation 3:17); the warning “lest he walk naked, and they see his shame” (Revelation 16:15) is aimed at a way of life, not a state of undress.
When God judges a covenant-breaker, He strips her: “Thy nakedness shall be uncovered, yea, thy shame shall be seen” (Isaiah 47:3).
And Paul’s one dread for the day of resurrection is to be caught uncovered — “if so be that being clothed we shall not be found naked” (2 Corinthians 5:3).
The naked are those with no righteousness to show and no covenant to plead — exactly the man at the wedding, speechless in his bare skin before the king.

The wardrobe has a battle form.
Ask an AI how to put on the helmet of salvation, and you get the average of the pulpits:

The helmet of salvation is the confident hope and assurance of your salvation in Jesus Christ that protects your mind from doubt, fear, and lies, and you put it on daily by faith as you remember the gospel and fix your eyes on eternity.

A state of mind, self-administered: remember, feel assured, fix your eyes.
Now run the words through the whole of Scripture instead.
The phrase is not Paul's; it is a quotation, and its first wearer is not the believer:

And he saw that there was no man, and wondered that there was no intercessor: therefore his arm brought salvation unto him; and his righteousness, it sustained him.
For he put on righteousness as a breastplate, and an helmet of salvation upon his head; and he put on the garments of vengeance for clothing, and was clad with zeal as a cloke.

The armor is God's own war-dress, put on because no man could — which is what “the whole armour of God” (Ephesians 6:11) says when it is allowed to mean it: not armor from His stores, but the armor He wears, lent to the soldier.
And the Hebrew under “salvation” is the word this book met on the mountains of the Gospel chapter: yeshuah — the helmet of Yeshuah.
The head, covered with Him.

David had already defined the piece without naming it: “the strength of my salvation, thou hast covered my head in the day of battle” (Psalm 140:7) — a covered head, yeshuah, and a battle; and the covering verb is the sukkah root: a booth pitched over the head, and pitched by God's hand — “thou hast covered.”
And what covers a man's head? “the head of every man is Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:3).
The armor verbs are this chapter's verbs — clothing verbs — and their object is a Person: “put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 13:14).

The forehead seals it.
The high priest's mitre carried a graven plate “upon Aaron's forehead,” reading HOLINESS TO THE LORD, “that they may be accepted” (Exodus 28:36-38); the word is bound “as frontlets between thine eyes” (Deuteronomy 6:8); and the redeemed wear “his name… in their foreheads” (Revelation 22:4) — while the counterfeit is issued for the same head: the beast's mark “in their foreheads” (Revelation 13:16).
The helmet is the Name and word of Yeshua covering the mind; the enemy makes helmets too.

Scripture even stages the two armors side by side, in a fitting room before a duel.
Saul dresses David in his own gear — “and he put an helmet of brass upon his head” — and the shepherd takes it all off again: “I cannot go with these; for I have not proved them” (1 Samuel 17:38-39).
The word under “proved” is nasah — tested; the King James even says David “assayed to go” — and the armor of a man failed the assay.
David walks to the giant in what he had tested: “The LORD that delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me” (1 Samuel 17:37) — prove all things, hold fast that which is good, worn as battle-dress.

Mark the weight.
Man's armor is heavy on the wearer, and the tradition it stands for binds “heavy burdens and grievous to be borne” on other men's shoulders (Matthew 23:4).
God's armor runs the other way: “my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30); “his commandments are not grievous” (1 John 5:3) — and it is the armor of light (Romans 13:12).
In English the two senses share one word, and the pun is ours, not the Hebrew's: or is the light that shines, qal the light that weighs nothing, and the Greek splits them the same way. Even without the pun, the doctrine stands: the armor made of light is also the armor that is light, because the One who wore it first carries the weight.

Now walk down Paul's whole list with the Glossary of this book open: the girdle of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, the feet shod with the gospel of peace, the shield of faith, the helmet of yeshuah, and the sword of the Spirit, “which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6:17).
Every piece is a defined symbol: the whole armour of God is the symbolic vocabulary of Scripture, worn as clothing.
The milk reading arms a man with his own feelings; the word read whole dresses him in Christ from head to foot.

The symbol takes its place with the rest.
The gospel is the covenant announced; the way, the truth, and the life are the covenant embodied; the name is the covenant owned; and the garment is the covenant worn — righteous acts done, granted in the blood of the Lamb and kept clean to the end.

The marriage of the Lamb is set, and the call has gone out to many.
But “many are called… few are chosen” (Matthew 22:14): the chosen are the few found on the highway of holiness, properly dressed.
The one who walks some other road, or comes to the feast in a covering of his own cut, is the man without a garment — speechless at the door, and cast into the dark.
And how a covenant binds not one wearer but a whole people together is the next symbol: the bow.
